Calculate \(\Delta H\) for \(C(s) + CO_2(g) \rightarrow 2CO(g)\) using: \(C(s) + O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)\), \(\Delta H = -393.5 \, \text{kJ/mol}\); \(CO(g) + \frac{1}{2}O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g)\), \(\Delta H = -283 \, \text{kJ/mol}\).

text_solutions:
The \(\Delta H_f\) for CO can be found from the second reaction: \(\Delta H_f (CO) = \Delta H_f (CO_2) + 283 = -393.5 + 283 = -110.5 \, \text{kJ/mol}\).

For the target reaction: \(\Delta H = 2 \times \Delta H_f (CO) - \Delta H_f (CO_2) = 2 \times (-110.5) - (-393.5) = -221 + 393.5 = 172.5 \, \text{kJ/mol}\).

text_solutions: For adiabatic compression, \( T_2 = 400 \times (20/5)^{0.4} \approx 400 \times 1.741 = 696.4 \, \text{K} \). Then, \( \Delta T = 696.4 - 400 = 296.4 \, \text{K} \). Internal energy change: \( \Delta U = nC_v\Delta T = 1 \times 20.785 \times 296.4 \approx 6160 \, \text{J} \).

qns_content.text: A system absorbs 1200 J of heat and does 500 J of work on the surroundings at constant pressure. What is \(\Delta H\)?

text_solutions: At constant pressure, \(\Delta H = q_p\). Here, \(q = 1200 \, \text{J}\) (heat absorbed), so \(\Delta H = 1200 \, \text{J}\).

text_solutions: Multiply first equation by 2: \(2C(s) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow 2CO_2(g)\), \(\Delta H = -787 \, \text{kJ}\). Reverse second: \(2CO_2(g) \rightarrow 2CO(g) + O_2(g)\), \(\Delta H = 566 \, \text{kJ}\). Add: \(\Delta H = -787 + 566 = -221 \, \text{kJ}\).
